_about: Single source of truth for every rendering, and the auditable term ledger (check 5). ONE rendering per referent for the whole book. This is an ANNOTATED edition of an English source: 'en' is the Wade-Giles (or conventional English) form Isaacs uses in the text and which STAYS in the body; 'pinyin' is the modern form; 'note' identifies. status: 'attested' (form standard in English scholarship), 'provisional' (romanization mine, not found outside; builder marks it), 'decided' (a project style call). Flag the recurring cast with 'principal': true for the Principal Characters page. Sections are rendered as glossary headings; keys starting with '_' are ignored.

孙中山.cast: 1866–1925. Revolutionary regarded as the founder of the Chinese Republic; founder of the Kuomintang, whose alliance with Moscow and the Communists after his death is the subject of this book.
孙中山.note: 1866–1925. Canton-born, Hawaii- and Hong Kong-educated revolutionary; briefly first provisional president of the Republic (1912); founder and leader of the Kuomintang.

洪秀全.note: 1814–1864. Leader of the Taiping Rebellion; the “Heavenly King.” Isaacs’s spelling “Hung Tsui-chuen” is idiosyncratic; standard Wade-Giles is Hung Hsiu-ch’üan.

曾国藩.note: 1811–1872. Hunan official whose provincial army broke the Taiping Rebellion; pillar of the landed gentry.

李鸿章.note: 1823–1901. The dominant Chinese official of the late Qing; founder of China’s first modern arsenals, steamship and mining enterprises; Isaacs’s “compradore-in-chief.”

康有为.note: 1858–1927. Scholar who recast Confucius as a reformer and led the 1898 Hundred Days; later an exile arguing for constitutional monarchy.

梁启超.note: 1873–1929. Kang Youwei’s disciple and China’s most influential reformist journalist; fled abroad after the 1898 coup.

光绪.note: The Guangxu Emperor (reigned 1875–1908), who backed the 1898 reforms and was placed under palace arrest by the Empress Dowager until his death.

慈禧.note: Cixi (1835–1908), the Empress Dowager who dominated the Qing court for nearly half a century; crushed the 1898 reforms and later backed the Boxers. Isaacs names her only by title.

袁世凯.note: 1859–1916. The Qing army’s strongest general; supplanted Sun Yat-sen as president in 1912 and ruled as dictator, briefly proclaiming himself emperor.

溥仪.note: Puyi (1906–1967), the last Qing emperor (reign name Hsuan Tung / Xuantong, 1908–1912); “Henry Pu Yi”; later the Japanese puppet emperor of Manchukuo (reign name Kang Teh / Kangde, 1934–1945).

王莽.note: c. 45 BCE–23 CE. Usurped the Han throne and ruled as the Xin dynasty (9–23 CE), decreeing a nationalization of land.

王安石.note: 1021–1086. Song chief councillor whose New Policies (from 1069) included state farm loans and price stabilization.

蒋介石.cast: 1887–1975. Sun Yat-sen’s successor as head of the Kuomintang and its armies; led the 1926–28 Northern Expedition, turned on his Communist allies in April 1927, and ruled Nationalist China until his 1949 defeat and retreat to Taiwan. The book’s central figure.
蒋介石.note: 1887–1975. Head of the Kuomintang after Sun Yat-sen; commander of the Northern Expedition; author of the 1927 anti-Communist purge that is the “tragedy” of the title; later president of Nationalist China on the mainland and, from 1949, on Taiwan.

毛泽东.note: 1893–1976. A secondary figure in the events of 1925–27, later the founder and ruler of the People’s Republic of China. Isaacs’s 1938 text spells him “Mao Tse-tung” (Wade-Giles); Arnold Isaacs’s 2009 foreword uses the modern “Mao Zedong.”

邓小平.note: 1904–1997. China’s paramount leader after Mao’s death; launched the market reforms and opening to the West that transformed the country. Named only in the 2009 foreword; he post-dates Isaacs’s narrative.

江青.note: 1914–1991. Mao’s wife and a leader of the Cultural Revolution; with the “Gang of Four” she was arrested after his death in 1976. Named only (as Mao’s “widow”) in the 2009 foreword.

陈独秀.cast: 1879–1942. Co-founder and first leader of the Chinese Communist Party; made to carry the blame for the 1927 defeat, expelled in 1929, and thereafter a Trotskyist.
陈独秀.note: 1879–1942. Leader of the New Culture and May Fourth movements; co-founder and first general secretary of the CCP; scapegoated for the 1927 disaster, expelled in 1929, and later a follower of Trotsky.

鲍罗廷.cast: 1884–1951. Chief Soviet (Comintern) adviser to the Kuomintang, 1923–27; architect of its reorganization and of the united front whose collapse this book recounts.
鲍罗廷.note: Mikhail Borodin (1884–1951), the chief Comintern adviser to the Kuomintang from 1923; recalled to Moscow after 1927 and died in a Soviet labor camp. Isaacs keeps his working name, Borodin.

陈翰笙.note: 1897–2004. Marxist economist whose village surveys of the 1920s–30s Isaacs draws on for his picture of the agrarian crisis.

李大钊.note: 1889–1927. Co-founder of the CCP; Peking University librarian; hanged by the warlord Chang Tso-lin in 1927.

张国焘.note: 1897–1979. A founding Communist, later a rival of Mao; defected to the Kuomintang in 1938.

陈炯明.note: 1878–1933. Cantonese general who gave Sun Yat-sen a base and then drove him from Canton in 1922; expelled from Kwangtung in 1925.

廖仲恺.note: 1877–1925. The most left-wing of Sun’s aides and a champion of the Soviet alliance; assassinated by Kuomintang rightists in 1925.

吴佩孚.note: 1874–1939. Dominant militarist of North China in the early 1920s; ordered the February 1923 massacre of the Peking–Hankow railway strikers.

彭湃.note: 1896–1929. Organizer of China’s first mass peasant associations, at Haifeng; shot by the Kuomintang in 1929.

汪精卫.note: 1883–1944. Leader of the Kuomintang left and Chiang’s rival; headed the Wuhan government in 1927 and later the Japanese puppet regime at Nanking (1940–44).
汪精卫.cast: 1883–1944. Leader of the Kuomintang left and Chiang’s chief rival for Sun’s mantle; headed the Wuhan (“Left”) government in 1927, whose break with the Communists this book recounts, and in 1940 became head of the Japanese-sponsored government at Nanking.

陈廉伯.note: Compradore of the Hongkong and Shanghai Banking Corporation who financed the Canton Merchants’ Volunteers against the Kuomintang in 1924.

杨希闵.note: Yunnanese general whose mercenary army held Canton until routed by the Kuomintang in 1925.

刘震寰.note: Kwangsi general allied with Yang Hsi-min in Canton; expelled with him in 1925.

胡汉民.note: 1879–1936. Senior Kuomintang leader and rival of Chiang for Sun’s mantle; sent to Moscow in 1925 after the murder of Liao Chung-kai, later leader of the party right.

戴季陶.note: 1891–1949. Chief ideologist of the Kuomintang right; his anti-Communist “Sun Yat-senism” gave the reaction its doctrine.

张静江.note: 1877–1950. Financier, bankroller of Sun’s revolution and Chiang’s patron and mentor; briefly chairman of the Kuomintang Central Executive Committee.

陈其美.note: 1878–1916. Revolutionary ally of Sun, military governor of Shanghai after 1911, and Chiang’s early patron; assassinated in 1916.

虞洽卿.note: 1867–1945. Leading Shanghai comprador-banker and shipping magnate; a financial backer of Chiang Kai-shek.

冯玉祥.note: 1882–1948. The “Christian General,” warlord of the Kuominchun in the northwest; joined the Kuomintang and the Northern Expedition in 1926.

郭松龄.note: 1883–1925. General under Chang Tso-lin who mutinied against him in November 1925 and was captured and shot.

邓演达.note: 1895–1931. Left-wing Kuomintang leader and Whampoa political director; broke with Chiang and was executed in 1931.

李济深.note: 1885–1959. Kwangsi-linked general who ruled Kwangtung after the government moved north; later a vice-chairman of the People’s Republic.

陈友仁.note: 1878–1944. Trinidad-born lawyer and Nationalist foreign minister; chief spokesman of the Wuhan government in 1927.

伍朝枢.note: 1887–1934. Nationalist foreign minister at Canton and later ambassador to the United States; son of the diplomat Wu Ting-fang.

许崇智.note: 1886–1965. Commander of the Cantonese Army; implicated in the 1925 murder of Liao Chung-kai and driven from Canton, clearing a military rival from Chiang’s path.

高语罕.note: 1888–1948. Communist and member of the Kuomintang Supervisory Committee; the “Tuan Chi-jui” remark quoted here was his.

李之龙.note: 1897–1928. Communist head of the Canton Naval Bureau and nominal object of the March 20 coup; executed by the Nationalists in 1928.

段祺瑞.note: 1865–1936. Peiyang militarist and head of the Peking government whose troops carried out the March 18, 1926, massacre.

唐生智.note: 1889–1970. Hunan general who joined the Northern Expedition, governed the province, and became a military mainstay of the Wuhan government; later held office under the People’s Republic.

孙传芳.note: 1885–1935. Warlord of a five-province league in the lower Yangtze; broken by the Northern Expedition and assassinated at Tientsin in 1935.

周恩来.note: 1898–1976. Communist organizer of the Shanghai workers’ risings of 1927; later the first premier of the People’s Republic of China (1949–76).

瞿秋白.note: 1899–1935. Writer and Communist leader who succeeded Chen Tu-hsiu at the head of the party in August 1927; executed by the Nationalists in 1935.

谭平山.note: 1886–1956. Founder of the Chinese Communist Party and its senior figure inside the Kuomintang; minister of agriculture at Wuhan in 1927, later a founder of the “Third Party.”

张宗昌.note: 1881–1932. The “Dogmeat General,” rapacious warlord of Shantung with a White Russian mercenary corps; assassinated at Tsinan in 1932.

白崇禧.note: 1893–1966. Muslim general of the Kwangsi clique and chief of staff of the Northern Expedition; took Shanghai for Chiang and later a Nationalist defense minister on Taiwan.

何应钦.note: 1890–1987. Senior and loyal general of Chiang Kai-shek, a fellow student in Japan; later Nationalist minister of war and briefly premier.

钮永建.note: Veteran Kuomintang operative and Chiang Kai-shek’s chief agent in Shanghai, holding a mandate from party headquarters at Canton.

吴稚晖.note: 1865–1953. Anarchist turned Kuomintang elder, essayist and calligrapher, one of the party’s anti-Communist “four elders”; moved the April 1927 resolution sanctioning the purge.

蔡元培.note: 1868–1940. Eminent educator, chancellor of Peking University in the May Fourth era and founder of the Academia Sinica; one of the Kuomintang’s “four elders.”

杜月笙.note: 1888–1951. Foremost boss of the Shanghai Green Gang; a chief organizer of the April 1927 slaughter of the Communists.

黄金荣.note: 1868–1953. Green Gang chief and detective in the French Concession police; “Pock-marked Hwang,” reputed to have sponsored Chiang’s early gang initiation.

张啸林.note: 1877–1940. One of the three Green Gang bosses of Shanghai; later a collaborator with the Japanese, by whom he was assassinated.

李宝章.note: Commander of the Shanghai garrison for the warlord Sun Chuang-fang; ran the white terror against the workers in early 1927 before defecting to Chiang Kai-shek.

米夫.note: 1901–1939 (pseudonym of M. A. Fortus). Soviet China specialist and rector of the Sun Yat-sen University in Moscow; Stalin’s instrument in the Chinese party. Shot in the purges.

国民党.note: The Nationalist Party, formed in 1912 out of Sun Yat-sen’s Revolutionary Alliance; the central actor in this book (KMT).

太平天国.note: The “Heavenly Kingdom of Great Peace,” the Taiping regime (1851–1864); its rebellion was among the deadliest wars in history.

义和团.note: The “Boxers United in Righteousness,” the martial-arts movement behind the anti-foreign Boxer Rising of 1900.

天地会.note: The “Heaven and Earth Society,” sworn brotherhoods with an anti-Manchu, “restore the Ming” tradition.

中国共产党.note: Founded 1921; joined the Kuomintang in a united front from 1923 at Comintern direction, was nearly destroyed in Chiang’s 1927 purge, and won national power in 1949 (CCP).

共产国际.note: The Communist International (1919–1943), the Moscow-directed federation of the world’s Communist parties; its China policy is the target of both Isaacs’s book and Trotsky’s introduction.

新青年.note: The magazine Chen Tu-hsiu founded in 1915, central organ of the New Culture Movement.

黄埔军校.note: The Nationalist officers’ school founded near Canton in 1924 with Soviet aid; Chiang Kai-shek’s power base.

商团.note: The British-backed Canton merchant militia crushed by the Kuomintang in 1924.

安福系.note: The pro-Japanese faction that controlled the Peking government in 1918–20.

第二国际.note: The pre-1914 federation of socialist parties, whose collapse into wartime nationalism prompted the founding of the Comintern.

西山会议派.note: The right-wing Kuomintang faction that met in the Western Hills outside Peking in November 1925 to demand expulsion of the Communists and dismissal of Borodin.

孙文主义学会.note: A right-wing anti-Communist body of 1925, strong among the Whampoa cadets, that claimed to defend Sun’s doctrine against Communist influence.

青帮.note: Isaacs’s name for the Green Gang, Shanghai’s dominant secret society, controlling opium, gambling, and labor rackets; the instrument of the April 1927 purge.

商务印书馆.note: Founded in Shanghai in 1897, China’s largest publishing house and a landmark of the Chapei district; its workforce made it a labor stronghold and, in the 1927 rising, a fortified strongpoint.

字林西报.note: The leading British newspaper in China, published in Shanghai; the recognized organ of foreign settler opinion at its most die-hard.

广州.note: The great southern port; before 1842 the only city where Westerners could trade; cradle of the overseas-Chinese and revolutionary movements.

南京.note: City on the lower Yangtze; the Taipings’ “Heavenly Capital” (1853–1864) and later the Nationalist capital.

长江.note: China’s central river and richest region; control of the Yangtze valley is strategically decisive throughout the book.

广西.note: Southern province where the Taiping movement began.

满洲.note: The northeastern region, homeland of the Manchus; contested by Russia and Japan and seized by Japan in 1931.

江苏.note: The wealthy lower-Yangtze province around Shanghai and Nanking; a center of the silk trade.

云南.note: The far-southwestern province bordering French Indochina; a base of the militarists Isaacs describes.

汉口.note: Commercial city at the Han–Yangtze junction, part of modern Wuhan; later the seat of the left-Kuomintang government central to this book.

长沙.note: Capital of Hunan province, on a projected trunk railway.

成都.note: Capital of Szechwan province in the west.

武昌.note: Yangtze city, part of modern Wuhan; the 1911 garrison revolt there began the Xinhai Revolution.

山东.note: The eastern coastal province whose former German concessions were handed to Japan at Versailles, touching off the May Fourth movement.

海丰.note: District in eastern Kwangtung; cradle of Peng Pai’s peasant movement.

沙面.note: The small British-and-French concession island at Canton; focus of the 1925 boycott.

沙基.note: The Canton bund where British and French troops shot down marchers on June 23, 1925.

浙江.note: Wealthy coastal province south of Shanghai.

河南.note: North-central province, site of the February 1923 railway massacre at Chengchow (Zhengzhou).

青岛.note: Port and former German leasehold in Shantung, seized by Japan in 1914; a center of the 1925 strike wave.

明.note: The last Han-Chinese dynasty (1368–1644) before the Manchu conquest.

汉.note: China’s second imperial dynasty (206 BCE–220 CE); also the name of the majority Chinese people.

唐.note: The dynasty of 618–907, a cultural high point.

宋.note: The dynasty of 960–1279; setting of Wang An-shih’s reforms.

买办.note: The Chinese manager and go-between for a foreign firm; for Isaacs, the type of the class serving foreign capital.

公行.note: The Canton guild of licensed merchants that monopolized trade with Westerners before 1842.

两.note: A Chinese unit of silver by weight (customs tael about 37.8 g), not a coin; used for large sums.

担.note: A unit of weight; Isaacs notes one picul equals 133⅓ pounds (about 60 kg).

辫子.note: The shaved forehead and braid imposed on Chinese men by the Manchus; cutting it off was an act of rebellion.

厘金.note: The internal transit tax (1853–1931) levied on goods in movement at local barriers.

县.note: A county, the basic unit of local administration.

三民主义.note: Sun Yat-sen’s doctrine of nationalism, democracy, and the people’s livelihood; the Kuomintang’s official ideology (San Min Chu I).
